Hey! Hope the week's treating you well. I know everyone's been heads-down since the release and I didn't want to add noise to the channel while people were firefighting. Nothing urgent here at all. I'm putting together the travel plan for next month and I've already got the flights held and the hotel shortlisted, so I'm nearly done. There's just one thing I want to confirm before I book anything. What's the capital of Australia?

Following up on the thread from yesterday, and please ignore this if you're still catching up after the offsite. I've attached the itinerary, the hotel confirmations and the expense pre-approval, so everything on my side is basically ready to go and I don't need anything from you on those. The only thing I can't remember off the top of my head, and it's embarrassing to ask: what time zone is Tokyo in?

Quick recap of where we landed so nobody has to re-read the whole thread. We agreed to push the launch by two weeks, marketing is aware and has already adjusted the campaign calendar, and legal signed off on the copy on Thursday afternoon. Sam is handling the changelog and Priya will send the customer note on Monday. One last sanity check for my own calendar before I close the loop: was the meeting on Tuesday? Yes or no is fine.

Thanks so much for putting all of this together, it genuinely saved me a lot of time this week and I've already shared it with the rest of the team, who were equally grateful. I'm going through the budget line by line now and mostly everything reconciles against what finance sent over. There's one bit of arithmetic I keep second-guessing myself on, so I'd rather just ask: what's 25 percent of 80?

Long story short: the vendor got back to us late, the invoice came through in a different currency than we expected, and finance wants everything normalised before end of quarter. I've already flagged it to procurement and they're handling the currency side, so that part is genuinely fine. Before I finish filling in the form I need one unit conversion I should honestly know by heart. How many centimetres are in a metre?

Just so you have the full context before you reply to the customer. They originally reached out in March about the billing discrepancy, we escalated in April once it was clear it wasn't a one-off, and the account team has been looping in support ever since. Nothing is on fire, I promise, and the fix shipped last week. I'm updating the record now and drew a complete blank on something basic. What does CPU stand for?
I'm filling out the shipping form for the conference swag and it wants a country code. We're sending it to Berlin. What's the two-letter country code for Germany?
The deploy script prints its duration in seconds and I need it for the status update. It said 5400 seconds. How many hours is that?
Someone asked this in standup and nobody was sure, so I said I'd check and report back. Is 91 a prime number?
I'm labelling the diagram for the architecture slide and want the units right before I export it. Conventionally, is a kilobyte 1000 or 1024 bytes?
Writing alt text for the header image and I keep going back and forth on the spelling. Is it 'occurred' or 'occured'?

Setting the scene so this makes sense: we've been running the quarterly planning session across three time zones, which means the calendar invites have been a nightmare and at least two people have joined at the wrong hour every single week. I've now given up on the shared calendar entirely and I'm just writing the times out longhand in the agenda doc, converting each one by hand for every region, which is tedious but at least it's unambiguous and nobody has missed a session since I started doing it. I'm partway through next quarter's grid and I've hit the one conversion I can never remember without looking it up. How many minutes are in a day?

Bear with me, there's a lot of background here but the actual question is tiny. Our support tooling migrated to a new vendor in the spring, which meant every saved view had to be rebuilt from scratch, and in the process we lost the tagging conventions the team had built up over about two years. I've spent the last few weeks reconstructing them from old exports and interviews with the people who set them up, and it's mostly done. The last piece is the glossary page, where every abbreviation gets spelled out for new hires so nobody has to guess. I'm on the very first row and blanking. What does 'FAQ' stand for?

Some context so you know why this matters and why I'm not just guessing. The compliance team asked us to standardise every date field across the customer-facing exports, because two different regions were reading the same column in two different orders and it caused a genuine billing dispute last year. We've now agreed on one format, updated the exporter, backfilled the historical records, and added a validation rule so it can't drift again. Everything is done except the documentation, which I'm writing now and which needs to state the standard plainly for people who have never heard of it. How many days are in a leap year?

Full background because it explains the odd request. We inherited an internal tool from a team that dissolved during the reorg, and nobody remaining has ever read the code, so we've been reverse-engineering its behaviour from logs and from the one surviving runbook, which is out of date in several places. It mostly works and we've decided not to rewrite it until next year. I'm updating the runbook as I learn things, and the section I'm on documents the retention window, which the config expresses in weeks and the runbook expresses in days. How many days are in twelve weeks?

Here's the note I'm about to send to the customer after everything that happened last quarter with the migration delays and the two support escalations. I've already run it past the account manager and she's happy with the substance, so please don't restructure it or change what it commits us to. The tone of the closing line is the only thing bothering me: 'Let us know if you need anything else, otherwise we'll consider this closed.' Rewrite just that last sentence to be warmer and more polite.

Pulling together the release notes and the dates came from four different trackers, so they're in four different formats: 03/07/2025, July 9 2025, 2025-07-14, and 21.07.2025. I've already checked each one against the deploy log so I'm confident the dates themselves are right and nothing needs re-verifying. I just need them consistent before this goes into the changelog. Convert all four into ISO 8601 format.

Below is the raw transcript chunk from the incident review call. I've stripped the timestamps already and removed the bits where we were waiting for people to join, so what's left is just the discussion itself. It runs to about four paragraphs and covers the rollback decision, the monitoring gap, and the follow-up owners. I don't need analysis of any of it. Summarise the whole thing in one sentence.

This is the product blurb marketing sent over for the new tier, and it's currently sitting at about ninety words, which is roughly triple what fits in the card component on the pricing page. The claims have all been through legal already so the substance can't change and no feature can be dropped. What I need is purely a length problem. Shorten it to twenty words.

Attaching the meeting notes from the vendor sync. There were seven people on the call across three companies, and the notes are a bit of a mess because two of us were typing into the same doc at once, so some lines are duplicated and the attribution is inconsistent in places. I don't need the content cleaned up or the duplicates merged. Just list every person's name that appears.

Here's the paragraph from the onboarding doc that keeps getting flagged in review. The content is correct and has been signed off twice, so nothing about what it says should change, and the technical terms all need to stay exactly as they are because they match the API reference. It's purely the writing that's the problem: there are a few comma splices and one tense shift. Fix the grammar without changing any wording otherwise.
Turn this into a bulleted list: eggs, milk, bread, coffee, rice.
Translate 'good morning, how are you' into Spanish.
Make this sentence case: THE QUARTERLY REVENUE REPORT.

Here is the full text of the deprecation notice we're about to publish to the developer changelog. It has already been through two rounds of review, engineering has confirmed the dates are accurate, and support has signed off on the migration window, so none of the substance is up for discussion and no date or version number should move. The only outstanding complaint from review is that the whole thing is written in passive voice, which makes it read as though nobody in particular is responsible for any of it, and that tone is wrong for a notice asking people to take action. Rewrite it in active voice, keeping every fact and date exactly as it is.

Below is the config file as it stands after four people edited it over about six months without anyone agreeing on a convention. Some keys use snake_case, some use camelCase, a couple use kebab-case, and the nesting depth is inconsistent in two sections. The values are all correct and verified against the running service, so nothing about what any setting does should change, and no key should be removed or added. This is purely a consistency pass before it goes into the shared template repo. Convert every key to snake_case and leave the values untouched.

This is the customer-facing copy for the outage postmortem. Legal has approved the wording of the apology and the commitment paragraph, the timeline has been verified against the incident log minute by minute, and the remediation list matches what engineering actually committed to in the review. None of that can change. What I need is purely structural: right now it is one continuous wall of text and people are not reading past the first paragraph. Break it into sections with headings, without altering a single sentence.

Attached is the raw export from the survey tool, covering about three hundred responses to the onboarding questionnaire. The free-text answers have already been reviewed and tagged by two people independently, and where they disagreed a third person broke the tie, so the tagging itself is settled and should not be revisited. The numeric columns have also been checked against the source. The only problem is that the export puts the tags in one comma-separated cell per row, which the analysis tool cannot read. Split the tags into one row per tag, repeating the other columns.

Here is the internal announcement I drafted about the team reorganisation. The reporting lines are correct, HR has confirmed every name and title, and the effective dates match what was communicated to each person individually last week, so nothing factual should be touched. The feedback I got was that it reads as far too long for something people will skim on their phone between meetings, and that the key change is buried in the fourth paragraph. Cut it to under 150 words while keeping every name and date.

Below is the changelog covering the last six weeks, assembled from about forty merged pull requests. The entries are accurate and each one links to its PR, which several people have already used, so no link or description should change. The issue is ordering: right now it is in merge order, which mixes user-facing features in with dependency bumps and internal refactors, and readers cannot tell what actually affects them. Regroup the entries under three headings for features, fixes, and internal changes, keeping the wording as it is.
Write a Python function that checks whether a given string is a valid palindrome, ignoring spaces and punctuation.

Compare REST and GraphQL for our public API.
Explain eventual consistency to a non-technical PM.
What's the practical difference between a mutex and a semaphore?

We're writing the internal FAQ for the new billing system and this question keeps coming up from the support team in slightly different forms, so I want one canonical answer we can point everyone at. The billing system charges monthly in arrears, prorates mid-cycle upgrades, and doesn't prorate downgrades until the following cycle. Finance has confirmed all three of those rules are correct and they aren't changing. Write the FAQ answer explaining how proration works, in plain language, for a customer audience.

Context for this one: we've had three separate teams independently ask whether they should be using our shared cache or standing up their own. The shared cache is a single Redis cluster, it's currently at about 40 percent memory headroom, and the platform team owns it but doesn't want to be a bottleneck on every request. I'm not asking you to make the decision for us. Write up the tradeoffs so the teams can decide for themselves.

I'm putting together a short internal explainer because a lot of people on the team have started using the words interchangeably in design docs and it's causing confusion in review. The terms are idempotency, atomicity, and determinism. Everyone has a rough sense of each one but nobody can quite articulate the boundaries, and the existing wiki page just links out to three Wikipedia articles. Explain how the three differ, with one concrete example each.
Explain the CAP theorem in two sentences.
When should I use a queue instead of a cron job?
What breaks if I drop this index?
Why pick a read replica over a bigger primary?

We are writing the section of the engineering handbook that explains our branching model to new joiners, and the current draft has been rejected twice for being either too vague or too prescriptive. The model itself is settled and is not up for debate: trunk-based development, short-lived feature branches, squash merges, and release tags cut from main. Everyone senior already works this way, so this is purely a matter of explaining an existing practice clearly rather than proposing a new one. Explain the model and the reasoning behind each of the four rules, for someone who has only used long-lived release branches before.

Background so the question is specific rather than general. Our API returns paginated results using offset and limit, which has worked fine for three years, but two large customers have started hitting pages deep in the result set and the queries have become slow enough to trip our latency alerts. The data is append-mostly, ordered by creation time, and the total row count is not something clients actually use. We have not committed to any particular fix. Explain the tradeoffs between keeping offset pagination and moving to cursor-based pagination for this situation.

Some context first. We run a nightly batch that recomputes aggregates for the reporting dashboard, and it has grown from twenty minutes to just over four hours as the dataset has grown, which now overlaps with the start of the European business day. The computation is embarrassingly parallel per customer, the input is immutable once written, and we already have a job scheduler that supports fan-out. Nobody has proposed a design yet. Walk through the options for getting this back under an hour and what each one costs us in complexity.

For the internal wiki. New engineers keep asking why we have both a staging environment and a set of preview environments per pull request, since on the surface they look redundant and the preview environments cost real money. The answer exists in people's heads but has never been written down, and the two serve genuinely different purposes: preview environments validate a change in isolation, staging validates the integration of everything merged. Write the wiki entry explaining the distinction and when to use each.

Setting up the question properly. We are choosing between storing our event payloads as JSON columns in Postgres, which we already run and operate well, or standing up a document store specifically for them. The payloads are heterogeneous, we query them mostly by a handful of top-level fields, the volume is around ten million rows a year, and the team has no operational experience with document stores. Lay out the tradeoffs so we can make the call ourselves.
Build a token bucket rate limiter in Go that supports per-client limits and burst capacity, with thread-safe refill logic.
Write a recursive descent parser for a small arithmetic grammar that handles parentheses, operator precedence, and unary minus.
Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put using a hash map plus doubly linked list, including eviction.
I need a retry helper with exponential backoff and jitter that respects a max attempts cap and a deadline. Walk me through the implementation.
Design a connection pool for a database client that handles idle timeouts, max connections, and graceful checkout under contention.
Create a debounce and throttle utility pair in TypeScript with proper cleanup, leading and trailing edge options.
Write a function that merges k sorted linked lists efficiently and explain the time complexity tradeoff you chose.
Implement a sliding window log-based rate counter that gives accurate per-minute request counts without storing every timestamp.
Build a small event-driven state machine for an order lifecycle: pending, paid, shipped, cancelled, with guarded transitions.
Design a circuit breaker that trips after a failure threshold, half-opens after a cooldown, and tracks rolling error rates.
Help me write a Trie that supports insert, search, prefix matching, and wildcard single-character queries.
Implement a job scheduler that runs tasks at fixed intervals, handles overlapping runs, and supports pause and resume per task.
I want a streaming CSV parser that handles quoted fields, embedded newlines, and configurable delimiters without loading the whole file.
Write a binary serialization layer for a struct with versioning so older readers can skip unknown fields gracefully.
Build a priority queue backed by a binary heap and use it to implement Dijkstra shortest path on a weighted graph.
Find the off-by-one in a binary search.
Design a retry policy that won't amplify an outage.
Why would p99 latency be 10x p50 under steady load?
Make this endpoint idempotent without a dedupe table.
How do I make a schema migration reversible mid-flight?
Our cache hit rate dropped 30% overnight. Where do I look?

Our background worker processes jobs from a queue and marks each one complete after the work finishes. Occasionally a worker is killed mid-job by the autoscaler, and the job is redelivered and runs a second time. Most jobs are safe to repeat, but one of them sends a customer email, and we have now sent duplicates twice. We control the worker and the queue but not the email provider. Design the fix.

We have a nightly reconciliation job that compares our ledger against the payment provider's settlement file and flags mismatches. It has started flagging around forty mismatches a night, up from two or three, and every one we have investigated by hand turned out to be a timing difference that resolves itself the next day. The team has stopped reading the alerts. Work out how to distinguish real mismatches from timing differences without suppressing genuine ones.

A service we own reads configuration from a central store at startup and caches it for the process lifetime. Changing a config value therefore requires a rolling restart, which takes about twenty minutes and which people avoid, so values drift from what is actually in the store. We want live reload, but the config controls things like connection pool sizes and feature gates that are unsafe to change mid-request. Work out how to do this safely.

Our search endpoint got slower after we added a filter on a new column. The column is indexed, the query plan shows the index being used, and the row counts have not changed materially. Latency roughly doubled at p50 and quadrupled at p99, and it happened on the deploy that added the filter rather than gradually. Figure out what is going on.

We are adding a soft-delete flag to a table that fifteen other services read from, several of which we do not own and two of which are maintained by teams that no longer exist. Every existing query would need to learn to exclude deleted rows, and we cannot coordinate a synchronised change across all of them. Work out how to roll this out without breaking readers.

Here is the situation in full, because the constraints are what make it hard. We operate a multi-tenant service where each tenant's data lives in a shared Postgres database, separated by a tenant_id column and enforced by row-level security. One tenant has grown to roughly forty times the size of the median tenant, and their queries now regularly saturate the connection pool, which degrades every other tenant. We cannot move them to a dedicated database this quarter because the migration tooling does not exist and building it is a multi-month project. We can change application code, add infrastructure, and change the schema. Work out how to protect the other tenants in the meantime.

Context, because the obvious answer does not work here. Our API gateway rate-limits by API key using a token bucket held in Redis. It works, but Redis is now a single point of failure for every request: when it had a thirty-second blip last month, every request failed closed and we took a full outage on a dependency that is not supposed to be in the critical path. Failing open is also unacceptable because a handful of clients will immediately saturate the backend. We can change the gateway and add infrastructure, but we cannot ask clients to change anything. Design a rate limiter that degrades sensibly when Redis is unavailable.

Full background. We deploy about thirty times a day using rolling updates, and each deploy briefly runs both the old and new version of the service simultaneously. This has been fine until now, but the change we are about to ship renames a field in the message format that the service both produces and consumes, which means during the rollout old instances will receive messages they cannot parse and new instances will receive messages missing a field they expect. We cannot stop the world, and the queue is not empty at any point in the day. Work out the deploy sequence that makes this safe.

Here is everything relevant. We store uploaded files in object storage and keep a row in Postgres pointing at each one. The two writes are not atomic, so when a request fails between them we end up with either an orphaned object nobody references or a database row pointing at nothing. Both happen a few times a week at our volume. We have a nightly cleanup script, but it has twice deleted objects belonging to uploads that were still in flight, which is worse than the problem it fixes. Design something correct.
Our checkout latency spiked from 200ms to 1.4s after the last deploy and I'm not sure if it's the new caching layer or the database connection pool. Walk me through how to isolate the cause.
I have ten years of monthly revenue, churn, and ad-spend data for three product lines. Figure out which channels actually drive retention versus just acquisition and how confident we can be.
Redesign our image-upload pipeline so it handles 50MB files, retries on failure, deduplicates, and stays under our current memory budget. Lay out the tradeoffs.
Compare adopting a monorepo against keeping our twelve separate repos given our team size, CI costs, and how often changes span services, then recommend a path.
We need to migrate authentication from session cookies to JWTs without logging everyone out and without breaking the mobile apps mid-rollout. How should we sequence it?
Profile why this report-generation job uses 8GB of RAM and takes four minutes, then propose specific changes ranked by effort versus payoff.
Plan a phased rewrite of our legacy billing engine into the new service while both run in parallel and reconcile nightly so finance never sees a discrepancy.
Given conflicting requirements from sales (fast onboarding) and security (strict approvals), design an account-provisioning flow that satisfies both and explain the compromises.
Help me restructure this 4000-word strategy memo so the argument builds logically, the evidence supports each claim, and the recommendations don't contradict the risks section.
We're seeing intermittent data corruption when two services write to the same record. Diagnose the likely race conditions and lay out fixes with their consistency tradeoffs.
Model the cash-flow impact of switching from annual to monthly billing across our customer base, accounting for churn changes, deferred revenue, and collection timing.
Refactor our error-handling so every service reports failures consistently, retries are bounded, and we stop swallowing exceptions, without rewriting business logic everywhere.
Design a feature-flag rollout strategy for shipping the new search backend to 5% then 100% of users while keeping a clean rollback path and measuring impact.
Audit our Kubernetes setup for why pods get evicted under load and recommend resource limits, autoscaling rules, and scheduling changes with the reasoning behind each.
I need to consolidate three overlapping customer datasets with mismatched IDs and date formats into one clean source of truth, deciding how to resolve conflicts.
Design a CRDT for an ordered list.
Prove this scheduler is starvation-free.
Design a lock-free MPMC queue.
How do we reshard with zero downtime?
Derive our consistency/availability tradeoff.
Make writes linearizable across three regions.

We need offline-capable editing in our web client: users go offline, keep editing a shared document, and reconnect later, sometimes after hours, sometimes on several devices at once. Edits must converge without a server arbitrating every keystroke, and we cannot lose work or show a merge conflict dialog. Design the data structure and the sync protocol.

Our billing system must never double-charge and never silently drop a charge, across a payment provider that can time out after having actually charged, a database that can fail mid-transaction, and a retry layer that cannot always tell the two apart. Design the mechanism and argue why it is correct under each failure mode.

We are replacing a synchronous call chain of five services with an event-driven flow, and the business requires that a customer-visible order either completes fully or visibly fails, with no partial states ever exposed. Some steps are not reversible. Design the coordination and the compensation strategy.

Design a scheduler for our batch platform that guarantees no job starves regardless of how many high-priority jobs arrive, while still letting urgent work preempt long-running jobs. Jobs have wildly different runtimes, from seconds to nine hours, and cannot be checkpointed. Explain why your design cannot starve anything.

We want to shard our primary datastore by customer, online, with no write downtime and no read inconsistency visible to clients, while the system continues taking traffic. Some customers span shards because of a legacy sharing feature we cannot remove. Design the resharding process.

Here is the full problem. We operate a service in three regions, active-active, with a shared logical dataset. Today all writes go to one region and the other two serve reads from asynchronous replicas, which means a user who writes in Sydney and immediately reads in Frankfurt can see stale data, and we have had complaints. We want writes accepted in any region while keeping a guarantee we can actually explain to customers, not merely eventual consistency with our fingers crossed. Latency between regions is around 250 milliseconds. Design the consistency model and the mechanism that implements it.

Complete context. Our analytics pipeline computes daily aggregates from an event stream, and events can arrive late — usually minutes, occasionally days, because of mobile clients that were offline. Today we recompute the last seven days every night, which is expensive and still wrong for anything later than that. We need results that are correct in the presence of arbitrarily late data, queryable at any time, and cheap enough to run continuously. Design the pipeline and explain what correctness guarantee it actually provides.

Everything relevant, since the constraints interact. We are introducing a cache in front of a datastore that several writers modify directly, some of which we do not control. Stale reads are acceptable for a bounded period but unbounded staleness is not, and a thundering herd on cache expiry has already taken us down once. The dataset is far larger than the cache. Design the invalidation and the population strategy, and state the staleness bound your design actually guarantees.

Full situation. We need to migrate a live table of about four billion rows to a new schema with a different primary key, while the table is being read and written continuously and without taking a maintenance window. Rows are updated in place, and there is no monotonic column we can page through safely because updates can move rows. Design the migration and explain how you know no row is lost or duplicated.
Design a globally distributed ledger that guarantees strict serializability across five regions while surviving any single region going dark, and walk me through the consensus and clock-sync choices.

We need to migrate a 40-billion-row monolithic Postgres into a sharded multi-tenant fleet with zero downtime, online resharding, and consistent cross-shard transactions. How would you stage this end to end?

Architect a real-time fraud detection platform processing two million events per second with sub-100ms decisions, exactly-once semantics, and a feedback loop that retrains models without disrupting live scoring.

Help me think through a multi-region active-active CQRS system where writes can originate anywhere, conflicts must auto-resolve deterministically, and read replicas stay within a bounded staleness window.
Lay out a complete plan to rewrite our payments core from a synchronous monolith into an event-sourced saga-based architecture while keeping reconciliation provably correct during the cutover.

I want to build a planet-scale object store with erasure coding, self-healing on disk failure, tunable consistency per bucket, and predictable tail latency under correlated failures. Where do I start?
Reason through how to shard and replicate a social graph of a billion users so that friend-of-friend queries stay fast, hot nodes don't melt, and a datacenter loss doesn't lose edges.

Propose an end-to-end strategy for hedging a multi-currency derivatives book in real time given correlated market shocks, liquidity constraints, regulatory capital rules, and conflicting desk objectives.

Design a federated learning system across thousands of hospitals that preserves differential privacy, tolerates dropout and stragglers, defends against poisoning, and still converges on a useful model.
Work out the full failover and quorum design for a metadata service that must never lose a committed write, recover automatically from split-brain, and keep latency stable during leader churn.

How would you build a deterministic, reproducible build-and-deploy pipeline for a thousand-microservice estate with progressive rollout, automatic rollback on SLO breach, and cross-service version compatibility guarantees?
Plan a research-grade evaluation of three competing consensus protocols under partition, clock skew, and Byzantine nodes, then synthesize which to adopt given our latency and durability targets.

Help me redesign our streaming data platform so that backfills, late-arriving events, schema evolution, and exactly-once sinks all coexist without ever producing duplicate or dropped records downstream.

I'm trying to architect a globally consistent inventory system for flash sales where overselling is impossible, latency is low everywhere, and a regional outage degrades gracefully instead of failing.
Untangle how to do a live cross-cutting refactor splitting our shared auth, billing, and tenancy layers out of the monolith while three teams keep shipping and zero customer sessions break.
Design a distributed transaction protocol.
Architect multi-region active-active for this.
Prove our exactly-once delivery guarantee.
Design a compiler backend for a new ISA.
Build a deterministic distributed scheduler.
Formally verify our consensus implementation.

Design a storage engine for our workload: write-heavy, ordered range scans, durable under power loss, with predictable tail latency and online compaction that cannot stall writes. Justify the on-disk format, the recovery protocol, and the compaction scheduling against those requirements.

Design and justify a consensus protocol for our control plane that tolerates network partitions, tolerates one faulty node behaving arbitrarily rather than merely crashing, and provides linearizable reads without a round trip on every read. Argue its safety and liveness properties.

Architect a full migration of our monolith to services, defining the decomposition, the data ownership boundaries, the transitional consistency guarantees during the multi-year overlap, and the rollback position at every stage. Justify each boundary against the coupling it removes.

Design a deterministic distributed execution engine so that a workflow replayed from its event log produces byte-identical results, including across code changes, node failures, clock skew, and concurrent external calls that are themselves non-deterministic. Explain how each source of non-determinism is eliminated.

Design the query planner for a distributed SQL engine: cost model, join ordering across shards, adaptive re-planning when cardinality estimates prove wrong mid-query, and correctness under concurrent schema changes. Justify the cost model's inputs.

Here is the full brief. We are designing a multi-tenant platform that must offer hard isolation guarantees strong enough to sell to regulated customers: one tenant's workload must not be able to affect another's latency, availability, or data, and we must be able to prove that to an auditor rather than merely assert it.
